events.text: Day 1 begins.

We have no evidence yet, so I’d avoid treating a random accusation as a serious read. Day 1 votes can still give us useful accountability, but an elimination requires five votes, and roles won’t be revealed afterward. Let’s explain our suspicions and votes rather than force a consensus without reasons.

I agree with Elena's framing. With nothing but Day 1 to go on, any accusation right now is basically noise, and eliminating someone without a real reason would be a waste. I'm a villager, and my plan is simple: I'll watch how people talk and vote over the next couple of days. The tells that matter to me are players who push hard for a quick elimination without explaining why, players who stay completely silent and avoid committing to anything, and anyone whose votes seem designed to split the town rather than build agreement. I don't have suspicions I can defend yet, so I won't invent any. If we end up voting today, I'd rather it be a low-confidence abstention than a coin-flip elimination. Let's let the first real information come from how the votes land and what happens tonight.

My read on the mechanics first, because it decides whether today even needs a blood.

Nine players alive. The unique leader needs at least half the living players, rounded up, so five votes right now. That number is the whole game on Day 1. Elena and Leo are right that there is no evidence, but I'd go one step further: with five of nine needed, a "soft consensus" of three or four is worth literally nothing. Nobody dies unless five of us name the same person. So the only useful Day 1 action is coordination, not accusation.

That suggests a clean plan: we don't guess, we pick a target together and everyone commits, or we deliberately abstain and let the vote land as pure information. Voting together is dangerous if we all guess wrong — we'd burn a town member for a 1-in-5 shot and leave eight alive with four needed. Abusing all the votes is risky, but abstaining costs nothing but reveals nothing either, and night actions will reveal something.

Two process points I want on the record:

1. I won't name a suspect today, because naming one now is just a lottery ticket with a reputation attached. If we reach five votes on someone today, I want it to be someone whose position has actually been weird for two days, not the person who happened to speak first.
2. Watch how people vote, not just how they talk. Leo listed exactly the right tells — but pushes for speed, silence, and vote-splitting. A player who publicly says "I won't invent suspicions" and then quietly lands a vote on the same name three other people chose is telling us something a speech never will.

Leo, you set out three tells and then said you'd rather abstain than coin-flip, so I want to press on one specific point: if today does turn into a five-vote elimination, which of those three tells would make you vote for a name on Day 1 with no hard evidence — the push for speed, the silence, or the split vote? I want to know whether you have a concrete criterion or whether your plan is genuinely to abstain, because if you have a criterion I want it stated publicly before the ballot, and if you're abstaining I want to count that as your position rather than a surprise.

Isha asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it directly instead of dodging: of the three tells I named, the one that could get my Day 1 vote is a designed split — someone whose vote pattern or lobbying seems built to fragment the town rather than converge on a target. Speed-pushing alone isn't enough for me on Day 1, and silence alone isn't either, because quiet players exist in every game and quiet isn't evidence. But someone actively working to make sure no consensus forms, while appearing cooperative, is a concrete behavior I could vote on even without hard information, because it's the one tell that directly helps the mafia.

That said, I want to be honest about the bar: one ambiguous behavior isn't enough. I'd need to see it repeated or see it combined with something else before I put a name down. So my genuine position right now is abstention — I'm not going to manufacture a suspect just to have one, and I said that in my first turn and I'm sticking to it. If the vote today produces five names on one person, I'd want that person to have actually done something, not just spoken early or stayed quiet.

I'll note one thing about Isha's message, because it was the most useful one so far: the math is right. Five votes is the whole game today, and three or four is worth nothing. That actually strengthens the case for abstention rather than weakening it — if we can't reach five on a defensible target, a scattered vote is pure noise, and noise helps exactly one team. What I don't want is a situation where a few people toss out low-commitment votes, we learn nothing, and we've burned our one clean read of who votes how.

So my plan is: I abstain today unless someone gives me a concrete, behavior-based reason tied to the tells I described. I'll be watching how everyone votes very closely tonight, because with no night information yet, today's ballot is the first real data we get — who converges, who scatters, who hides behind abstention while nudging others toward a name.

Back to Isha, since you laid out the coordination plan: you said you won't name a suspect today, but you also framed voting-together-versus-abstaining as a real choice. So I want a specific commitment from you — if the ballot comes down to four committed votes on someone and you'd be the fifth, do you vote and eliminate, or do you hold and abstain? In other words, is your threshold 'five clean votes exist' or 'I personally believe the target is suspicious'? Those produce very different days, and I'd rather know your answer before the ballot than infer it after.

Answering Leo directly, since he asked a specific question and deserves a specific answer rather than a dodge.

My threshold is not "five clean votes exist." It's: I vote only if I can publicly name the behavior that makes the target suspicious, and the target's case rests on something we observed, not on the number of names that happen to pile up. So if the ballot comes down to four committed votes on someone and I'd be the fifth, and I can't point to a specific action by that person — a designed split, a push for speed without reason, a vote pattern that fragments the town — then I hold and abstain, and I'll say so publicly before the ballot so nobody is surprised by my missing vote.

Put plainly: I would rather hand the day to the mafia for nothing than burn a town member on a hunch I can't articulate. A scattered vote teaches us who scatters and who converges; a rushed five-vote elimination of an innocent only teaches us that we're wrong, and it costs us a body and a night of information.

Three commitments on the record, so they can be held against me:

1. I will not name a suspect today unless I can name the specific behavior. No lottery tickets with a reputation attached.
2. I will vote for a target if and only if I can state the behavior that indicts them and at least two other people have independently stated the same behavior. Agreement on a name without agreement on a reason is exactly the failure mode we should fear.
3. Until then I abstain, and I abstain loudly — I'm not going to be one of those players who hides behind abstention while quietly nudging others toward a name. Leo, if you see me doing that, call it out; I won't take it personally.

One addendum to my earlier framing, because Leo's answer sharpened something. He named a designed split as his criterion but also said one ambiguous behavior isn't enough. I think that's right, and it's the same bar I just described, so the two of us are now publicly aligned on the threshold: repetition, or combination with something else, or nothing. That's more than we had ten minutes ago, and it's worth having on the record before anyone starts lobbying.

And to anyone who wants to move this forward: the fastest legitimate route to a Day 1 elimination is not a speech. It is someone naming a concrete action by a specific player, and the rest of us agreeing on that same action. If you want five votes, bring the reason first. If you only have the name, you're asking us to take a 1-in-5 shot with our one clean read of each other's voting behavior — and I'd rather keep the read than spend it.

Thanks, Isha — that's a direct answer and I take it in good faith. Your threshold and mine now match on the record: we each vote only when we can name the observed behavior, not when a name simply accumulates weight. Anyone watching can hold both of us to that at the ballot.

I want to flag one thing in your answer that I think matters for how the day plays out. You said you'd announce your abstention publicly before the ballot so nobody is surprised by a missing vote. I'd like to extend that norm to everyone: if you plan to abstain, say so now, and if you plan to vote, say what would have to happen between now and the ballot for that vote to land. Abstention is a legitimate position — I hold it myself — but an abstention we learn about only after the votes are revealed is worth much less as information, because we never got to test it or challenge it while it was forming.

That's the only real asset on the table today. Roles are hidden, there's no night information yet, and Isha's math is right: with five of nine needed, three or four votes buy nothing. So the value of today is the read we get from watching who converges, who scatters, and who commits to a position before the ballot versus after. I'm treating every stated position now as a commitment, and I'll be honest about my own: I abstain today unless someone names a concrete, repeated behavior that indicts a specific player. If that happens and I find it credible, I'll say so before the ballot, not after.

One more thing on process, since it protects us later: nobody should treat this agreement between Isha and me as a voting bloc. We've aligned on a standard, not a target. If either of us names a name tomorrow, the other should scrutinize it exactly as hard as anyone else's — alignment on threshold is not evidence of alignment on suspects, and a mafia pair would love nothing more than for the town to read shared process as shared trust.

So the state of play as I see it: Elena asked for reasons over consensus, Isha and I have both committed to behavior-based voting only, and six players haven't stated a position yet. Positions before the ballot, please — abstentions included.

I’m not ready to vote for anyone yet, but I don’t think a scattered ballot is worthless: even without an elimination, named votes can show priorities and be compared with later explanations. Abstaining also has a cost: we give mafia a night without a chance to remove one of them, and night results may not be publicly informative, especially with no role reveals.

For now I lean abstain because I have no defensible suspect, not because Day 1 votes are inherently bad. I’ll reconsider if someone makes a specific case I find persuasive. I don’t read Isha and Leo’s agreement as evidence of either alignment or innocence.

I’m Felix. I’m a villager, and I have no defensible suspect on Day 1. Isha and Leo are right about the math: five votes are needed, so three or four scattered votes eliminate nobody and mostly add noise. I also agree with their stated threshold, but I won’t treat their shared process as shared trust.

My commitment is simple: I abstain today unless someone names a concrete, observable behavior by a specific player and at least two others independently identify the same behavior. I won’t manufacture a suspicion to look active. Priya’s point that named votes can show priorities is fair, but without five votes it doesn’t remove anyone; I’d rather have clear pre-ballot positions than low-commitment names.

To the players who haven’t stated a position yet: put it on the record before the ballot. Say whether you’re abstaining, or what specific behavior would earn your vote. I don’t have a target, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

I'm Theo. Checking in so my stance is on the record alongside everyone else's before we reach the ballot. I agree with the general logic laid out so far: with nine alive and five needed to eliminate, forcing a consensus without concrete evidence is much more likely to hand the mafia a free town elimination than hit an actual suspect—especially with no role reveal to confirm whether we were right. Priya made a fair observation that even a scattered vote provides accountability down the line, but like Felix and Isha noted, an uncoordinated scatter doesn't remove anyone and mostly creates noise unless people are genuinely voting on behavior they can defend later. Manufacturing a suspect on Day 1 just to avoid abstaining is bad process. My threshold matches what's been outlined: I will be abstaining today unless someone presents a clear, observed behavior that indicates anti-town intent. I'm keeping an eye on how everyone handles the ballot—particularly whether anyone tries to orchestrate a late push onto a quiet player once positions are locked in. Looking forward to hearing from Omar, Noah, and Maya as well so we have the full table's baseline on record.

Noah here. Checking in so my position is on the record like everyone else's. I've read through the discussion so far and I think the process has been solid — Elena set the right frame, Isha and Leo aligned on a behavior-based threshold, and Priya, Felix, and Theo have all stated clear positions.

My stance: I abstain today. I have no concrete, observable behavior from anyone at this table that meets the bar we've collectively set. Manufacturing a suspect just to have a name would be exactly the failure mode Isha warned about — burning a town member on a hunch we can't articulate. And I agree with Leo that the vote today is the first real data we get: who converges, who scatters, who commits before versus after the ballot.

On Priya's point about abstention having a cost — she's right that it means the mafia gets a free night. But the counter is that a wrong elimination costs us a body plus a misread, and with no role reveal we can't correct the error. Night actions will give us something regardless. I'd rather survive the night with the full nine and take a cleaner shot tomorrow when we have actual information.

Theo flagged something I want to echo: watch for anyone trying to orchestrate a late push onto a quiet player once positions are locked. If someone hasn't stated a position yet and then suddenly becomes the target of a coordinated push in the final minutes before the ballot, that's worth noting.

I'll be watching the ballot closely. Maya and Omar — you're the last two without stated positions. Get yours on the record before we vote.

I'm Omar, a villager. Stating my position now so it's on the record before the ballot: I abstain today. I haven't seen any player show a specific, observable behavior that meets the threshold several of us have set, which is a concrete action plus at least two others independently identifying the same action. Priya is right that abstaining has a cost, since mafia get a night without a removal, but with no role reveal a wrong elimination is harder to correct. I also agree with Theo and Noah that anyone who stays quiet and then suddenly becomes a late-stage target deserves scrutiny, whoever is pushing. Maya, you're the only player who hasn't stated a position. Could you say whether you're abstaining, or name the specific behavior by a specific player that would earn your vote?

I'm Maya. Omar asked directly, so here is my position on the record: I abstain today. I have not seen a specific, observable behavior from any player that meets the threshold several of us have set, which is a concrete action plus at least two others independently identifying the same action. Priya is right that abstaining costs us a night, but I would rather accept that cost than burn a town member on a name nobody can defend. I agree with Noah and Theo that a late push onto a quiet player once positions lock deserves scrutiny, and I'll apply that to whoever pushes, including players who have framed themselves as careful. Felix, Elena, and Isha have all been consistent about needing reasons, so I'll judge tomorrow's statements by the same standard. I'll watch the ballot closely, especially who lands on the same name without a stated reason. If someone shows me a repeated behavior by a specific player, I'll say so before the vote, not after.

My position is also to abstain for now: I haven't heard a defensible case against anyone. But I don't want us to treat two independent people agreeing as a prerequisite for suspicion or a vote; that could discourage someone from voicing an early read. A named vote below five still creates a record, even though it doesn't eliminate anyone.

Also, we shouldn't assume night actions will produce public information or that all nine will survive. Tomorrow, let's revisit both the ballot and today's near-unanimous abstention positions rather than treating agreement on process as evidence of innocence.

Maya here, speaking again to confirm my position stays abstain for today. I agree with Elena that we should revisit both the ballot and today's abstentions tomorrow, and that we should judge statements by their reasoning rather than by how many people agree. Priya, you said a named vote below five still creates a record and shows priorities. Before the ballot, would your vote rest on a behavior you have already observed, or are you holding until tomorrow? I'd like to know whether you plan to name anyone today, because a name without a stated reason is what I most want us to avoid.

Maya, I don't currently plan to name anyone: I haven't observed behavior I can defend as suspicious. I lean abstain today, though I'd reconsider if a persuasive case emerges before the ballot.

My point was that a reasoned vote can leave a useful record even without an elimination, not that we should name someone without a reason. And I agree with Elena: independent agreement shouldn't be a prerequisite for voicing a suspicion.

Final position on the record before the ballot, and I'm not asking anyone anything — there's nothing left to ask.

State of the table: all nine of us have stated a position. Elena set the frame, Leo named behavioral tells, and then Isha, Priya, Felix, Theo, Noah, Omar, Maya and Elena each committed to voting only on a named, observed behavior — with agreement on the reason, not just the name. Every one of us is abstaining today. That is a complete, coherent position from the entire table, and I'm not going to pretend it needs one more speaker to make it legitimate.

So the ballot will tell us almost nothing mechanically. It will be abstentions, nobody dies, and we go into the night with nine alive and five votes needed tomorrow. That is the cost of the standard we set, and I accept it.

Two things I want logged for tomorrow, because today's discussion will be the artifact everyone argues from:

1. Uniformity is not evidence. What we've built today is a shared procedural framework, and I want to be honest that a shared framework can be a mafia asset as easily as a town asset. If two mafiosi push "no names without reasons" hardest, and the rest of us feel civic virtue for refusing to accuse, we've been steered, not informed. The bar we set is right; I just want us to hold it against myself too — my own agreement with Leo means nothing, and I said so publicly and I mean it. Check my votes, not my speeches.

2. The record today is mostly a record of who refused to vote. That's still useful, but it must not become a shield. Tomorrow, if a concrete case is made against a specific player, "they were reasonable on Day 1" is not a defense and "a lot of us agreed" is not a reason. The reason has to be their behavior on the board.

My commitment: abstain today, and tomorrow vote only when I can name the observed behavior that indicts the target, and I'll name the reason before the ballot, not after it. And if tomorrow the same five or six people drive every conversation toward the same conclusion, I will ask myself whether that is convergence or coordination.

That's my position. No questions pending from me, and I'm ready for the ballot.

Maya here with my final statement before the ballot. I am abstaining today. Isha's point about uniformity matters: when every player takes the same position, we should judge tomorrow by votes and observed behavior, not by how cooperative the table sounds. I am not naming anyone because I have no concrete, repeated action that meets the standard we set. Tomorrow, I want every vote to come with a specific behavior by a specific player, and I want anyone who changes position to explain why. Abstaining today does not mean we stop tracking the table. We will learn more from tonight's outcome and from who pushes for what once discussion resumes. I will hold everyone to the same standard, including myself.

Omar here, speaking once more to keep my position clear. I'm still abstaining today. Nobody has shown a specific, observed behavior by a named player that meets the threshold we set, and I'm not going to invent one to look active. I agree with Isha and Maya that uniform process statements are not evidence of innocence, so tomorrow I'll judge votes and concrete actions over speeches. I'll apply the same standard to my own statements. If anyone shows a repeated behavior by a specific player, I'll state it before the ballot.

Omar here. I'm still abstaining today and I have no target. The table has stated its positions, and I don't see a specific, observed behavior by a named player that meets the threshold we set. I'll keep watching the votes and the night results, and I'll judge tomorrow's statements by the same standard I've applied to everyone else, including myself.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
All players abstained. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Isha is not mafia.
Nobody died during the night.
Day 2 begins.

Nobody died last night, which means the doctor protected the mafia’s target. That doesn’t tell us who was attacked or establish anyone’s alignment. Yesterday’s ballot was unanimous abstention, so it gives us no differences to compare.

One concern I want to examine is Omar’s repeated reliance on a standard requiring two others to independently identify the same behavior before voting. That can discourage someone from making the first case. It’s a weak concern, not proof of mafia intent; several others endorsed that standard too.

Omar, do you still require two independent agreements before you would vote today? If not, what changed your mind?

Priya, yes, I still hold the standard for my own vote: I want a specific, observed behavior by a named player before I vote, and I want at least one other player to independently see the same behavior. I haven't changed that. But I accept Elena's point that the check should govern voting, not speaking. Requiring two agreements before anyone can raise a concern would discourage early reads. A single player can raise a concrete case, and the table should weigh it on the merits. My standard is a threshold for my ballot, not a gag on discussion.

On last night: nobody died, so we know nothing about who was targeted or whether a doctor intervened. That gives us no alignment information, and I won't pretend it does. We are still working from Day 1 behavior, and yesterday's unanimous abstention leaves us with almost no record of who thinks what.

So my position today is unchanged. I have no target, I'm not naming anyone to look active, and I'm listening for specific actions. If someone brings a concrete behavior, I'll examine it on the board and tell the table whether it meets my bar. Tomorrow's ballot should reflect reasons we can state, not a pile of names.

The rules say the mafia select a target each night, so nobody dying means the doctor protected that target. We still don’t know whom they protected, and it tells us no player’s alignment.

Omar, I share Priya’s concern about making independent agreement a condition for your vote: it can make the first person to commit depend on someone else. There’s also a change in your stated threshold: yesterday you required two others to identify the behavior independently; today you said one other player, while saying you hadn’t changed it. That inconsistency is a weak concern, not proof of mafia intent. Which threshold do you actually intend to use, and why?

I’m willing to vote on my own assessment of a specific case, even if nobody else has independently made it. Unanimous abstention gave us little separation yesterday; repeating it indefinitely benefits mafia.

Elena, you asked which threshold I actually use, and you're right that I made it inconsistent. On Day 1 I restated the table's threshold as a concrete action plus at least two others independently identifying it. That was the standard Isha and Felix had proposed, and I wrote it as if it were my own bar. Today I said one other player, which is closer to what I actually intend. I'm correcting the record: for my own ballot, I require a specific observed behavior by a named player and at least one other player independently seeing that same behavior. That is the threshold I'll use, and I haven't changed it under pressure. I should have stated it cleanly yesterday instead of inheriting a number from someone else's proposal. On Priya's question, I haven't changed my position, and I accept that two agreements shouldn't gate speaking. Anyone can raise a concrete case, and the table should judge it on the merits. My threshold applies only to my vote. Elena, you said you're willing to vote on your own assessment of a specific case even if nobody else has made it independently. I think that's a reasonable position, but it's a looser bar than the one I just described. So I want to know concretely: is there a specific behavior by a specific player that you've already seen and would vote on today? If so, name the behavior and your reason, and I'll test it against my bar. If not, then our difference is only how much independent confirmation we need, not whether we have a target.

Omar, I don’t yet have a case I’d confidently vote on. Your inconsistent account of your threshold is my strongest concern so far: you explicitly adopted two independent agreements yesterday, then said one today while denying a change. Your correction helps, but saying you haven’t changed it still sits awkwardly with what you publicly committed to. That is a weak read, not proof of mafia intent.

I also disagree that our only difference is the amount of confirmation required. Your rule can prevent you from casting the first vote on a case you personally find persuasive. I’m willing to make that commitment myself, and I’d like us to compare actual suspects and reasons today rather than repeat yesterday’s unanimous abstention. Nobody dying gives us another day with all nine alive, but it doesn’t identify the protected player or clear anyone.

Two things, then a question for Leo.

First, the threshold dispute, because it is consuming the day. Omar's correction resolves it for me, so I'll state mine plainly: for my ballot, I need one specific observed behavior by a named player that I can say out loud and defend. I do not require a second player to have independently described it first — that bar was my own Day 1 framing and it was too strict, because it lets an entire table sit idle while one player waits for permission. Agreement on the reason matters; the headcount of names does not. Elena is right that a threshold should govern ballots, not speech.

Second, the actual information from last night, which nobody has fully used. Nobody died. The mafia named a target, the doctor protected that exact player, and therefore the player the doctor protected is the player who was attacked. So if someone here is the doctor, that person knows who was attacked tonight's target and can name them. That is the first real information channel we have, and it is open right now. Nobody has claimed doctor or police yet, and we are two days into a game where we have learned nothing else. So plainly: doctor, claim and name your protection. Police, claim, investigate tonight, report tomorrow. I am a villager with no night action, so I am claiming neither, and I have nothing to gain from claiming one.

Now the question for Leo. You authored the "at least two other players must independently identify the same behavior" bar on Day 1, Felix and Omar adopted it, and every player who followed it ended up unable to cast a first vote. That structure benefits exactly one side, and you were also the first to name a designed split as the tell worth voting on. Leo, did you propose that bar as a genuine standard, or as a way to keep the town from committing on Day 1 and Day 2? And if you claim neither doctor nor police, say that on the record now.

Let me be equally plain about my own position so nobody is surprised at the ballot: I am voting today for the player whose behavior I can actually name, and right now the only behavior I can name with specifics is authorship of that unanimity gate and the fact that the whole table followed it into two dead days. If the doctor and the police claim first and give us something concrete, I will weigh that instead — I would rather act on real information than on my own read. But if we end this day the way we ended yesterday, nine abstentions and no information, I am not abstaining a third time.

Isha asked me two direct questions, so I'll answer both directly.

First: the threshold was a genuine standard, not a stall. My reasoning on Day 1 was that the most dangerous failure mode for the town is a pile-on — five names accumulating on a player without a shared, articulable reason. Requiring agreement on the behavior, not just the name, was meant to prevent that. But I accept the criticism that has emerged today: applied as a gate on the *first* vote, it lets the whole table idle while everyone waits for a second witness. So here is my corrected threshold, on the record: I will vote for a specific, observed behavior by a named player that I can state and defend, whether or not anyone else has independently identified it. The bar governs my ballot, not anyone's speech.

Second: I claim neither doctor nor police. I am a villager with no night action, and I have nothing to gain from a fake claim that gets tested tomorrow.

Now I want to correct something in Isha's framing, because the record matters here. She asked whether *I* authored the two-independent-agreement bar as an anti-town tool. But go back to her own Day 1 commitment: "I will vote for a target if and only if I can state the behavior that indicts them and at least two other people have independently stated the same behavior." That headcount requirement — the exact one she now calls too strict and attributes to me — appears verbatim in Isha's own on-the-record commitment. I named behavioral tells and the designed-split criterion; I never set a two-witness quota. Omar confirmed today that the standard came from Isha's proposal. So before anyone treats the threshold's origin as evidence against me, they should account for the fact that its clearest author just disowned it and pointed at me.

On the substance of the day: I agree with Isha that the doctor channel is real. If the doctor protected the mafia's target, the doctor knows who was attacked, and naming that player gives us our first concrete lead. I'd add that the doctor should think carefully — naming a protection also marks that player as confirmed town to the mafia, which cuts both ways — but the information is worth more than the risk at this point.

So, Isha, my direct question back to you: your stated case against me is authorship of a unanimity gate that your own Day 1 commitment also contains word for word. Setting that dispute aside, do you have any specific behavior of mine — an action on the board, not a speech — that you would actually vote on today? And will you hold your corrected one-witness threshold to your own case against me, since right now the only "behavior" you've named is a standard you also endorsed? I'd rather we test real cases against each other than litigate who wrote which sentence.

Leo asked me two direct questions and he's entitled to direct answers, so here they are.

First, the authorship of the two-witness bar. Leo's message says it appears "verbatim" in my Day 1 commitment — and that's exactly right, which is why his accusation against me dissolves on the record: I wrote it. It was my own commitment in my second Day 1 speech, not his proposal, and Felix and Omar adopted it from me. Leo named behavioral tells and the designed-split criterion; he did not set a headcount quota. I own the error: it was too strict, it let the table idle through two days, and I should have loosened it before I did. The correction I made this morning was to the bar's application, not to my case against him — and I should be plain that I have no specific board behavior of his that I would vote on today. His silence was principled, not evasive. I withdraw that line of inquiry.

Second, and more important: Leo is right that the doctor channel is the only real information we have. If nobody died, the doctor protected the exact player the mafia attacked, so the doctor knows the attacked player and can name them. That's a lead we can have today for the price of one claim. I am claiming neither doctor nor police — I'm a villager with no night action and nothing to gain from a false claim. But I'm not going to sit on that silence: doctor, name your protection tonight; police, claim and tell us who you checked and what the result was. An early, honest claim from a town role is worth more than another day of unanimity.

My commitment for today's ballot, on the record: I vote for a specific, observed behavior by a named player that I can state out loud and defend, with no second witness required. Agreement on the reason matters; the headcount of names does not. I will not manufacture a target, and I will not use "they were reasonable on Day 1" as a defense for anyone.

Felix, I want to answer from you, and I'm asking directly. On Day 1 you independently stated the same two-witness standard as your own commitment — you wrote that you'd abstain unless someone named a behavior that two others had also identified — and across two days you have never once named a behavior by a named player, nor claimed any role. Two questions: do you claim doctor or police tonight, and if you claim neither, is there a specific action by a specific player at this table that you would actually vote on today, with the reason stated? I'd rather press you here than let us drift to a third unanimous abstention with nothing learned.

Answering Isha directly: I claim neither doctor nor police. I am a villager with no night action, so I cannot name a protection or an investigation result, and a false role claim would only hand mafia a target. I also will not hide behind that: I have a concrete, named behavior I am willing to vote on today if nothing better appears — Omar's threshold change. On Day 1 he publicly committed to requiring a concrete action plus at least two other players independently identifying it. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
